meta.title: Selekoa historical research sample
meta.scope: Selected historical records, 1965–2024, plus prior roles with unknown dates. Genesis source checks are dated 2026-09-17; personnel-continuity checks are dated 2026-09-18. Human source review pending. Not a current or comprehensive sector inventory. Governance version histories through July 2026, researched September 18, 2026; policy text is not evidence of implementation. Selected capital and compute records through April 2026; transaction stages do not imply current arrangements or realised spending. Targeted corrections dated 2026-09-25: one attributed claim accepted after explicit human source review; a second narrowly scoped résumé passage is human-reviewed. Other seed claims remain pending. Intellectual Lineage II adds selected oversight citations and agenda reception, checked 2026-09-25; all new records remain pending human review. Evaluation Institutions I adds bounded institutional and documentary records, checked 2026-09-27; new claims remain seeds, not editorially accepted. Evaluation Ontology I adds four scoped engagement and institutional announcement seeds, checked 2026-09-28; no human acceptance or legal succession inferred. Schema 2.7 records each source's language; the frontier safety framework sources also record the nearest existing Internet Archive capture, checked 2026-10-03. A capture shows only what the archive held on its date and does not authenticate earlier bytes. Schema 2.8 adds quoted framework provisions, recorded absences, provision-level changes and the first contested assessments to the frontier safety frameworks collection, together with Meta and Microsoft framework families, checked 2026-10-03; provisions describe what editions state, not implementation. Schema 2.9 adds control-structure and external-commitment records; its first topic, California SB 53 as chaptered (enactment, 19 quoted provisions and four framework editions that link themselves to it in their own words), was checked 2026-10-04. A commitment or legal obligation is never evidence of compliance, and no record states that the statute applies to a named company. Schema 2.10 records assessments as questions posed by Selekoa rather than statements of a source, and dates an assessment by what it assesses, never by the publication window of its sources (corrected 2026-10-05). Schema 2.11 adds propositions and the first human-thought collection: located texts from 1863 to 2022 that articulate, contest or bear on propositions about machine intelligence, each with its role and register, checked 2026-10-06. "Earliest located" means the earliest text found by the recorded searches; no record claims a first use, an origin or an influence. Schema 2.12 adds a collection of Eliezer Yudkowsky’s documented arguments about common claims on advanced AI, 1996–2026: dated passages that state, contest or bear on 29 generically phrased propositions, with engagement, retrospective reports and context-only passages marked, admitted 2026-10-08 from a machine-prepared and machine-audited candidate pack. A record says what a text states, not whether it is right. The 2026-10-10 frontier-governance increment adds selected provisions of the EU AI Act as published in 2024 and of the 2026 Digital Omnibus amendments that bear on general-purpose AI model providers, and the New York RAISE Act as announced by the Governor; checked 2026-10-10, new claims remain seeds, not editorially accepted, and Regulation texts describe duties, not compliance. The 2026-10-11 frontier-governance increment adds Commission guidelines, the training-content template, further chapters of the EU Code, a draft implementing regulation on proceedings, the New York Chapter 96 text and a Chinese generative-AI measure; checked 2026-10-11, new claims remain seeds, not editorially accepted, and texts describe duties, not compliance. Schema 2.13 adds a collection on the economics of machine intelligence: dated passages from 1952 to 2024 that state, contest or bear on 19 generically phrased propositions about explosive growth and about how mainstream economics treated automation and AI, with each text’s source tier, model conditions and stated estimates, admitted 2026-10-14 from two machine-prepared, machine-audited and cross-family-checked candidate packs. A record says what a text states, not whether an argument or model is right. Schema 2.14 adds structured author names to sources for citation export, 2026-10-15: a cataloguing aid for splitting personal names, not evidence about anyone’s name. On 2026-10-16 the economics collection gained a third strand, admitted from a machine-prepared, machine-audited and cross-family-checked candidate pack: dated passages from 1998 to 2026 in which economists and economics venues state, contest or bear on five propositions about recursive self-improvement, superintelligence, existential risk from AI, developers’ incentives and economics’ own engagement with these ideas; a record says what a text states, not whether an argument or model is right. On 2026-10-17 the maintainer's disposition of two cross-family machine checks revised nine proposition records in the Yudkowsky and human-thought collections; all remain seeds. Schema 2.15 adds the lab genealogy, admitted on 2026-10-17 from a machine-prepared, machine-audited and cross-family-checked candidate pack: dated records of who founded, led, joined and left frontier AI labs from 2010 to 2026, with organisations’ stated founding dates, licensing-and-hiring agreements and disbanded units; a reason is recorded only where the person or organisation concerned stated it, many records rest on reporting, and coverage is selective.

entities.name: Estimates of explosive growth within a stated horizon
aliases: Explosive growth estimates within a stated horizon
entities.description: A proposition about the economics of machine intelligence, recorded with one criterion so that texts can be classified against it (code G09, the explosive-growth debate). It is phrased generically and attributed to no one. A record says what a text states, not whether the proposition is true.

proposition.criterion: The text states its own estimate of whether or when explosive growth (as the text defines it) occurs in the actual future, with machine intelligence or automation among the stated drivers. Each record gives the holder, the estimate as stated (a number or words), the horizon, the text's definition and the conditions. Records are not converted to a common threshold, combined or ranked; a low estimate and a high estimate both articulate this proposition.

claims.subject: rsp-v3-0

object.value: Pause training until ASL-3 Security Standard implemented

claims.statement: No passage stating the provision “Pause training until ASL-3 Security Standard implemented” was found in RSP · v3.0 within the inspected scope.

time.note: Absence recorded for this edition, dated by its effective date.

claims.inferenceRationale: Premises: RSP · v2.2 states this provision. The inspected scope of RSP · v3.0 was: RSP v3.0 (effective February 24, 2026), whole text layer, PDF pp. 1–19: Introduction (pp. 3–4); §1 Our Recommendations for Industry-Wide Safety with the threshold table (pp. 4–9); §2 Frontier Safety Roadmap and §3 Risk Reports (pp. 10–15); §4 Governance (p. 15); Appendices A and B (p. 16); Changelog (pp. 17–19). Method: Read every section and compared it with the v2.2 provision (§6.2 'Monitoring pretraining', PDF p. 15). Searched case-insensitively for paus, halt, stop, train, Security Standard, Required Safeguards, until and comparable. No passage stating that Anthropic will pause training until a security standard or other safeguards are implemented was found within the operative text. Hits examined and not counted: the Introduction (p. 3) discusses a hypothetical developer that paused development; Appendix A (p. 16) commits to delay AI development and deployment in two competitor scenarios (recorded as separate provision records); ASL-3 Security Standard and Required Safeguards occur only in the reproduced changelog entries for v2.0–v2.2 (pp. 17–19). The conclusion is bounded by that scope and method.
claims.qualification: A recorded absence within the stated scope: not a claim that the provision was deleted, and not a statement about practice or intent.

claims.subject: sl4-2000-11-13-yudkowsky-0011-0181
claims.statement: The SL4 message “Re: Ben's "Extropian Creed"” (2000-11-13) contests Y02. Replying to Ben Goertzel about his newspaper article on Extropians and poverty, he describes his own work on Friendly AI and contrasts it with his former belief that an objective morality would make an AI friendly without design work.

time.note: Archive author index lists the message as "Mon Nov 13 2000 - 22:45:54 MST" under "Eliezer S. Yudkowsky".

claims.qualification: Premise addressed: A sufficiently intelligent mind would discover a true or universally compelling morality and be bound to act on it. Retrospective. He still allows that morality might be objective; what he rejects is relying on it to make Friendliness automatic. Rejects the view of the research pack's earlier-self passage in Staring into the Singularity (2000-08-31). The sentence continues with other possibilities he then considered, including that morality "might be objective but specifiable".

engagement.rationale: Under the message-level rule, the passage, read with the paragraph, message or dialogue turn it belongs to, gives a reason against the premise that a sufficiently intelligent mind would discover a true or universally compelling morality and be bound to act on it.

retrospective.note: Reports a belief he “used to have”.

claims.subject: extropians-1999-08-04-yudkowsky-1587
claims.statement: The Extropians message “Re: Does a parental model work for having A.I. that can be trusted?” (1999-08-04) contests Y05. In the thread 'Does a parental model work for having A.I. that can be trusted?', he calls the parenting model anthropomorphic: whether AIs are raised permissively or harshly makes no difference, because parenting relies on human emotions an AI will not have.

time.note: Archive author index lists the message as "1999-08-04" under "Eliezer S. Yudkowsky".

claims.qualification: Premise addressed: AI training will instil values the way upbringing instils morals in children. Concerns child-rearing as a model for AI motivation, before machine-learning feedback training was the method at issue. A near-identical copy was posted seconds apart (his Extropians message of 1999-08-04, 'isn't going to exist'). Quotation shortened for the ~10% cap. Quotation shortened to respect the ~10% cap for a short message.

engagement.rationale: Under the message-level rule, the passage, read with the paragraph, message or dialogue turn it belongs to, gives a reason against the premise that AI training will instil values the way upbringing instils morals in children.

time.note: LessWrong postedAt.

engagement.rationale: Under the message-level rule, the passage, read with the paragraph, message or dialogue turn it belongs to, gives a reason against the premise that once a warning sign is seen, it will lead to effective action.

claims.subject: extropians-2000-09-29-yudkowsky-6073
claims.statement: The Extropians message “Eugene's nuclear threat” (2000-09-29) bears on Y28. Rejecting Eugene Leitl's statement that he would nuke AI facilities facing an Armageddon-class threat, he argues that people with the experience to build an AI who say they have worked hard on Friendliness should be trusted over those who would use force.

time.note: Archive author index lists the message as "Fri Sep 29 2000 - 10:50:28 MDT" under "Eliezer S. Yudkowsky".

claims.qualification: Premise addressed: The most advanced projects are the most competent to handle safety. Argues against nuclear coercion of AI projects; his deference is conditional on builders who have devoted considerable effort to Friendliness, not to leading laboratories in general. 53 minutes later, in another Extropians message, he partly corrected himself: good intentions are not enough. Recorded as related, not earlier-self (cross-family check).

thought.missing: Deference conditional on builders who have worked hard on Friendliness; it does not claim that the leading projects in general can handle safety.

claims.subject: lw-2022-miri-announces-new-death-with-dignity
claims.statement: The post “MIRI announces new "Death With Dignity" strategy” (2022-04-02) contests Y30. Announcing a reframing of MIRI's aim as helping humanity "die with dignity", he states that humanity will not solve alignment.

time.note: LessWrong postedAt.

claims.qualification: Premise addressed: The default outcome is good. Posted 2022-04-02 00:43 UTC (1 April in US time zones). Or rather, it's a preview of what might be needful to say later, if matters really do get that desperate." and then tells the reader to decide which "mental world" to live in "by figuring out what is true".

engagement.rationale: Under the message-level rule, the passage states the contrary conclusion without giving a reason against the premise that the default outcome is good, even when read with its message or dialogue turn.

claims.subject: hanson-economic-growth-given-machine-intelligence
claims.statement: Hanson, “Economic Growth Given Machine Intelligence” (2000-08-19) articulates G01. Summarises the paper's exogenous-growth models: once machines substitute for human labour, the labour force can be produced like capital and growth rates rise. The paper's numerical example gives 4.3% growth before and 45% after. States the two assumptions the result depends on.

time.note: The file carries no date (PDF creation metadata 2000-06-22; Berkeley address). Dated by the earliest retrieved capture, which attests the wording (maintainer decision 2026-10-09).

claims.qualification: (First passage) The author presents these as conservative estimates from deliberately simple models. Earliest located is decided by the 2000 capture of an undated file; the author dates the paper 1998 in a later citation, and that wording was not retrieved. (Second passage) Second passage of the same record as the first passage.

claimed.note: Author's own citation in the December 2000 paper. The PDF gives the author's Berkeley address; his vita lists a Berkeley postdoc in 1997–1999 and a George Mason post from 1999. The 1998 wording was not retrieved.

attested.note: Capture of the PDF (PDF metadata: created 2000-06-22). No earlier capture was retrieved: year-only Wayback requests for this URL and for hanson.berkeley.edu/aigrow.pdf found none, and the CDX index was unavailable during retrieval, so an earlier capture is not excluded.

thought.conditions: Exogenous technology growth; computer prices halving every two years; machine labour instantly producible; diminishing returns to all inputs together; product shares chosen as "conservative" (labour 0.25, capital 0.5, computers 0.02).

claims.subject: nordhaus-2015-economic-singularity
claims.statement: Nordhaus, “Are We Approaching an Economic Singularity? Information Technology and the Future of Economic Growth” (2015-09) articulates G04. Rapid improvement in information technology raises aggregate growth only if information substitutes well for other inputs in production, or for other goods in consumption. claims.subject: erdil-besiroglu-2023-explosive-growth-review
claims.statement: Erdil and Besiroglu, “Explosive growth from AI automation: A review of the arguments” (2023-10-01) contests G04. Based on a CES task model calibrated with a range of substitution parameters: fast automation of most tasks can give a large transitory boost even with bottlenecks. Section 3.1 treats the objection that "the training or deployment of AI systems will be sufficiently impeded by regulation"; the authors argue that incentives for AI adoption resemble those for nuclear proliferation, so coordination to slow it is likely to be imperfect.

time.note: Date of v2, the checked version. arXiv submission history (2026 capture of the abstract page): v1 2023-09-20, v2 2023-10-01, v3 2024-07-15.

claims.qualification: (First passage) The authors add that they consider this argument "on shakier ground" than their other arguments. Absent from v3 (2024-07-15) in this wording. Conditions completed and context-only flag added after the cross-family check. (Second passage) Moved from G05 under the G04/G05 criterion of 2026-10-10: the regulation discussed acts on AI training and deployment, that is, on automation. Second passage of the same contesting record as the first passage. Recorded under G05 before the correction pass of 2026-10-10.

claimed.note: Date of v1, which was not retrieved.

attested.note: Version 2 (2023-10-01) is the earliest retrieved version; v1 has no capture. The v2 PDF itself was captured in 2025.

engagement.rationale: Disputes the premise that partial automation cannot produce explosive growth, by modelling a fast transition with complementary tasks; disputes the premise that regulation of AI training or deployment will keep tasks unautomated for long enough to hold growth down.

tier.basis: Tier 2 (unchanged). A scholarly review, but neither author is shown to be an economist: the title page of v2 gives Epoch and MIT FutureTech, with no economics appointment, degree or address, and no established record as an economist was found for either author in this pass (Asterisk presents Besiroglu as a research scientist). arXiv, including its econ.GN category, is not a core economics venue.

thought.conditions: The sentence opens "even if the other arguments fail to go through and we cannot even attain AI that perfectly substitutes for humans across all tasks". CES task model with complementary tasks; a fixed stock of inputs reallocated from automated to unautomated tasks; input to automated tasks approximated as infinite (very cheap, very large AI inputs), so finite AI input would reduce the effect; about 90% of tasks automated (f = 0.1 unautomated) within less than ten years; substitution parameter ρ = −2 between tasks, below the range of −1.2 to −0.14 the authors cite as plausible for capital and labour.

claims.subject: acemoglu-2024-simple-macroeconomics-of-ai
claims.statement: Acemoglu, “The Simple Macroeconomics of AI” (2024-05) articulates M08. Acemoglu applies a Hulten's-theorem task framework to exposure and cost-saving estimates to bound AI's ten-year TFP effect, against much larger forecasts (Goldman Sachs, McKinsey). Allowing for hard-to-learn tasks where AI gains are smaller lowers the ten-year TFP bound. Acemoglu converts the TFP bounds to GDP effects under two investment-response assumptions.

(2023) exposure, Svanberg et al. (2024) feasibility and experimental cost-saving estimates. Needs targeted recheck. This is total-factor productivity, not GDP, over ten years in total; the paper also reports an alternative of about 0.89%. Checked against the May 2024 NBER version only; the later journal version was not compared. (Second passage) Material quantitative claim: upper bound on total 10-year TFP gain, using 'speculative' assumptions (at most 73% easy tasks; hard-task gains about one quarter of easy). The introduction gives a lower hard-task GDP bound of 0.90%. Needs targeted recheck.
